name: Acute Cholecystitis

likely: Anaerobes (Bacteroides) — more relevant in severe/gangrenous cholecystitis
pathogens.why: Acute cholecystitis pathogens reflect the same enteric flora seen in other biliary tract infections, dominated by gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae, with anaerobes becoming more relevant in more severe, necrotizing presentations.

investigations.why: First-line imaging — gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid support the diagnosis.
Typically mildly elevated; significant jaundice should prompt consideration of choledocholithiasis or cholangitis instead.
Leukocytosis supports the diagnosis and tracks response.
May identify bacteremia and guide de-escalation.

reason: Right upper quadrant pain with a positive Murphy's sign and fever, in the absence of jaundice, is consistent with acute cholecystitis (typically calculous). Antibiotics should be started alongside surgical consultation for cholecystectomy (early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment in most cases) — antibiotics are an adjunct to, not a substitute for, source control.
